genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the site manager learned her trade through an apprenticeship
her crew works on old buildings
clients mostly ask for surfaces made to look new
the footings of the buildings give way under the stories added on
the floors are held up by temporary props before anything else
the ground is probed to find hollows
the gaps in the masonry are closed only after the building is made safe
she turns down decorative finishes while the frame is still weak
she takes the client under the floor to show him the damaged beams
text: She started out as an apprentice on repair jobs, and today she runs a crew that puts old buildings back on their feet. Wherever she goes, the trouble is the same. Owners want fresh walls, while the footings underneath sag beneath the stories that somebody added on over the years. Her answer is a strict order of work. Her men prop the floors up with temporary posts first, then probe the ground for hollows. Only after that do the masons close the cracks and rebuild the bearings. This site manager turns down decorative work for as long as the frame is still weak, and the talks that follow can get sharp. When a client hesitates, she hands him a lamp and walks him under the floor, where the beams have gone soft and spongy with damp. The look on his face usually puts an end to the argument.

units: two neighboring buildings stand at the end of the same street
the first is all glass and hands back the sky
the second is low and laid up in fired brick
the old front keeps the marks of the hands that raised it
the tower is judged too regular in its geometry
the house offers worn thresholds and uneven corners
the old building is faulted for being cramped and run down
the low rooms hold the warmth better
the heavy walls soften the noise
text: Two buildings share the far end of one street, and the taller one looms over its neighbor without ever winning the argument. The first is glass from foot to roof; it hands the sky back at you like a cold mirror, holds the eye a moment, then lets it go. The second sits low and heavy, laid up in fired brick that the wind has smoothed, and it keeps you looking. Its face still carries the marks of the hands that raised it. The comparison soon favors the humbler one. The tower offers a flawless geometry; the old house offers worn thresholds, corners that lean, a porch that shelters. One you visit, the other you live in. People call the old building cramped and run down, forgetting that its low rooms hold warmth and its heavy walls take the edge off noise. Beauty here comes from use, not from line.

units: the writer sends his sister news of the work
three jobs are running at the same time
the broken tiles have been swapped out by the roofer
the joints around the flue have been filled with a soft mortar
every window opening has been sealed against drafts
a strip of tape has been laid along the fixed frame
the tradesman offers to partition the back room into a study
the added wall will be light board with no contact with the ceiling
the walls will take a lime wash before the cold season
text: Dear sister, here is the update on the house at last, just as I promised you. Three jobs are running at once, so I will take them one at a time, in order. On the roof, the roofer swapped out the tiles that had broken, then came back to fill the joints around the flue with a soft mortar that can move a little. On the windows, I decided to seal every opening against the drafts: foam pressed into the recess, a strip of tape along the fixed frame, and they are gone. Inside, the tradesman wants to partition the back room off into a study. The added wall would go up in light board and stop short of the ceiling, without touching it. The walls still need a wash of lime before the cold weather sets in. I will write to you again as soon as the roof frame has been checked. Give the children a hug from me.

units: the lead designer is asked to retrace how the operation went
a detailed record of the standing building opened the project
that survey took a whole season
the tests brought out a weakened timber frame
the schedule had to be rewritten after that finding
only the frailest part was taken down
the rebuilding went up on the footings that had been kept
the tightness of the site made the trades harder to organize
bringing the pipework back into service was the trickiest phase
text: Asked to retrace the stages of the operation, the lead designer begins with the survey work. Everything, she says, started with a full record of the standing building, taken room by room and carried across an entire season. What came next? The tests, she explains, showed a weakened timber frame, and the schedule had to be rewritten around that finding. On the technical choices, she reports that only the frailest wing was taken down, and that the rebuilding went up on the footings that had been kept. Asked about the obstacles, she points to the difficulty of keeping the trades apart on so tight a site. And what does she take away from the whole stretch? Not the heavy work, she answers, but bringing the pipework back into service, a phase finished well past the date that had been announced.

units: a carpenter explains to his apprentice that the door is rubbing
the fault comes from the movement of the shell and not from the door
fitting another door would give the same jamming
a mark on the threshold proves the settling is still going on
the apprentice offers to plane the bottom of the leaf
the carpenter accepts that stopgap
the bearing under the wall will have to be rebuilt afterwards
the rubbing will come back if the ground drops further
text: The carpenter told his apprentice that the door was rubbing because the shell of the house had shifted. The apprentice asked whether they should fit another one. No, the carpenter said: the fault sat in the ground, so a fresh door would jam in exactly the same way. He pointed to the scar the leaf had worn into the threshold, proof that the settling had not stopped. The apprentice offered to plane the bottom of the leaf. His teacher agreed, though he warned that the cut would ease the trouble without curing it, and that the bearing under the wall would have to be rebuilt afterwards. Since the ground was still dropping, he added, the door would catch again within a season or two. The apprentice wrote down the lesson: treat the cause, or the repair keeps coming back, and the bill with it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old builders wanted to roof a wide hall with no support in the middle
a flat stone cover snaps under its own weight
the answer found was to lean the blocks against one another
this shape sends the load out to the side walls
wooden supports carried the work while it was going together
those supports were taken away once the middle block was in place
the sideways push shoved the walls outward
masses of masonry were added against the walls to hold them
text: Picture builders who want to roof a huge hall without setting a single column in the middle. Their trouble is easy to see: stone is heavy, and a flat cover snaps as soon as you stretch it across. So they looked for another way. What they found was the vault. Lean the blocks against one another and the load slides out to the side walls instead of dropping straight down. Of course the thing has to be held while it goes together, which is why they set wooden frames underneath to carry the stonework until it closed on itself. Once the middle block dropped into place, the timber came away and the vault stood on its own. That left the sideways push, which shoved the walls outward, so they answered with thick buttresses. Clever, no? Every obstacle called for one more piece, and in the end the hall held.

units: the choice between timber and masonry turns on how the building is used
a brick wall banks the heat before giving it back
a timber wall warms quickly and cools just as quickly
the heavy answer suits rooms in use all the time
the light frame suits premises used now and then
masonry calls for drying time and a crew of many hands
timber parts turn up cut to size and go together without water
the costs of the two methods end up close
designers advise deciding on the feel wanted indoors
text: Timber or masonry? The question comes up on every project, and the answer turns mostly on how the building will be used. A brick wall banks heat: it warms up late, then hands it back when the night comes down. A timber wall does the opposite, climbing quickly in temperature and losing it again just as quickly. For a room that is in use around the clock, weight wins the argument. For premises opened only now and then, the light frame wins instead. The work on the site splits the two families as well. Masonry has to dry and calls for a crew of many hands, whereas timber panels turn up cut to size and go together without a drop of water on site. Costs, in the end, tend to meet somewhere in the middle. So designers suggest choosing on the feel you want indoors, and not on whatever is in fashion this season.

units: an elderly tenant is allowed to walk through the building before it comes down
the hall floor is broken and holds the print of the furniture carried out
the apartment doors are shut and marked with a chalk cross
a thin partition had already been torn into by the workmen
an old wall paper shows behind the split board
the roof frame at the top lets a thread of air through
the stair rail worn by use moves her more than the rest
she thanks the caretaker on her way out
she refuses to lift her eyes toward the front of the building
text: The day before the demolition, the oldest tenant in the building was allowed one last walk through the condemned building. She pushed open the hall door first, where the broken tiling still held the print of the furniture carried out weeks before. Then she climbed on toward the landings, counting the shut doors, each one of them marked with a cross in chalk. On the third floor she stopped at a thin partition the workmen had already torn into; behind the split board lay an old paper that nobody had ever scraped off. She finished under the roof, where the tired frame let a thread of air through. Nothing moved her quite like the stair rail, polished smooth by hands long gone. On her way out she thanked the caretaker, and then she refused to lift her eyes toward the tall gray front.

units: the crack must be opened down to sound material
the dust is taken out with a brush
the edges are wetted before the filler goes on
the powder must be tipped into the water and never the other way round
the paste is pressed into the hollow to drive the air out
the surface is smoothed with a wide blade running past each side
drying lasts at least one whole night with no heating
the hardened patch is then sanded and dusted off
a mineral paint is brushed on in two crossed coats
text: Start by opening the crack along its whole length with the point of a trowel, cutting back until you reach sound material underneath. Brush the groove clean of dust, then wet the edges lightly, because a filler laid on a dry face will let go later on. Mix the paste in a clean bucket, tipping the powder into the water and never the other way round. Work it in straight away, pressing hard so that the air is driven out of the hollow. Smooth it off with a wide blade, running a little past the crack on each side. Leave it to dry overnight at least, and do not heat the room to hurry it. Sand the hardened patch with a fine abrasive, dust it off again, and run your hand across to check that the join no longer catches under your fingers. Only then brush on a mineral paint, in two crossed coats.

units: entry to several buildings of a low lying district has been banned
the families put out of their homes have been moved into a communal hall
an underground body of water has been swollen by rain that would not stop
the sand carrying the footings has been washed out by that water
the ground has settled unevenly
stepped cracks have opened across the fronts
the experts judge that the old fabric could not take such a movement
the stairwells have been declared dangerous
resin injections are announced to avoid demolition
text: Access to several buildings in the low lying district was banned yesterday, and the families put out of their homes were moved into a communal hall. Technical services have known the cause for seasons. An underground body of water, swollen by rain that would not stop, has washed out the sand on which the footings rest. The ground has settled unevenly, opening stepped cracks across the fronts. The experts called in judge that the fabric, already tired, was in no state to take a movement of that size. The stairwells were declared dangerous as a direct result, and the evacuation was ordered on the spot. Owners are demanding a second opinion, since putting the buildings right would mean underpinning the footings. The local authority has announced resin injections, failing which demolition would become unavoidable.
